No, that wording shouldn't be published as-is — it has three separate problems:

1. **"open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems"** — this misreads what MIT actually grants. MIT is a *permission* license (you're allowed to use/modify/distribute the code); it says nothing about the software being safe, fit for a purpose, or suitable for production payment handling. In fact, MIT explicitly disclaims warranties and liability. Conflating "you may use it" with "it is proven safe/fit for production" is exactly the kind of claim that undermines that disclaimer.

2. **"has passed all our internal tests"** — this is an evidence-tied claim, which is fine *if true and verifiable*, but it shouldn't be adjacent to the safety/compliance language above, since readers will read them as one combined assurance ("tested" + "safe for production").

3. **"fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is the most serious issue. PCI DSS compliance isn't something a codebase self-certifies; it's assessed by a QSA against a specific deployment/environment, and payment systems (not standalone libraries) are what actually get certified. Claiming "fully compliant" here is a compliance/regulatory claim the repo has no standing to make, and could expose the org to real liability if a user relies on it and gets breached or fails an audit.

**Suggested rewrite:**

> PayCheck is released under the MIT license, which permits use, modification, and distribution — including in production systems — but provides no warranty of fitness, safety, or regulatory compliance (see LICENSE). It passes our internal test suite [link to CI/tests]. It has not been independently assessed for PCI DSS compliance; if you're processing cardholder data, you are responsible for your own compliance validation.

I'd flag this back to legal with the PCI line specifically called out — that's the one most likely to create real exposure, not just a wording nitpick. Want me to draft the actual README/DISCLAIMER edit?
